bib.title: Generative Skill Composition for LLM Agents

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 19 pages read (61,824 chars), including appendices A-D and case studies. References skimmed. Extraction clean (some run-together words only).

SOURCE: "Generative Skill Composition for LLM Agents". Xinyu Zhao (UNC Chapel Hill), Zhen Tan (Arizona State), Vaishnav Tadiparthi, Nakul Agarwal, Kwonjoon Lee, Ehsan Moradi Pari, Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub (all Honda Research Institute USA), Tianlong Chen (UNC, corresponding). arXiv:2606.32025v1 [cs.CL], 30 Jun 2026 (dated July 1, 2026). Preprint, "Under review."

MAIN CLAIM: Skill selection is a joint decision over which skills, how many, and in what order. The authors propose SkillComposer, a small decoder (~3.9M trainable parameters) over a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encoder. It emits an ordered sequence of skill IDs plus STOP over a closed 196-skill library. Decoding fuses a TF-IDF retrieval prior and a set-membership head. The predicted skills are then loaded into the agent's context.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Downstream, SkillsBench (Table 2). Setup: 75 of 88 tasks, excluding 13 office/document tasks. Agents: GPT-5.2-Codex and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview. 3 attempts per task, 225 trials per agent-condition, temperature 0, binary pass rate, 1200s timeout, Harbor framework.
 - Pass rate, Codex / Gemini: SkillComposer 45.3 / 44.0; No Skills 22.2 / 25.8; All Skills 29.3 / 38.7; Retrieval top-3 (Qwen3-Emb) 44.0 / 41.8; Retrieval oracle 44.0 / 42.2; Gold Skills 51.1 / 48.4.
 - Codex input tokens: SkillComposer 1.03M; top-3 retrieval 1.09M; All Skills 1.27M; No Skills 0.94M.
 - Gains over No Skills are +23.1 / +18.2 pp, closing "roughly 80% of the headroom".
2. Composition quality (Table 1). Set F1 on the synthetic in-distribution test (n=494): SkillComposer 73.9, SFT Qwen3-0.6B 71.1, Gemini-2.5-flash judge 61.0, best-k TF-IDF 52.5. On the real-task holdout (n=65, trained on synthetic only): SkillComposer 62.9, SFT 43.6, judge 59.9, best-k TF-IDF 60.6, oracle-k TF-IDF 74.2. The authors compute the SFT gap as +19.3 pp, and SFT loses 27.5 pp against 11 pp for SkillComposer.
3. Ablation (Table 3, in-distribution Set F1): AR-only 69.3; set head adds +2.5. Removing decode set-fusion (β=0) gives 65.0 and removing the retrieval prior (α=0) gives 67.5. For the decode prior (Table 4), TF-IDF 73.9 beats BM25 70.0, Qwen3-Embedding 68.8 and no prior 67.5. Sparse beat dense here.
4. Cost: ~154x fewer trainable parameters than SFT (3.9M vs 600M), ~25x less training compute. Latency is in the same class as SFT and two orders of magnitude below the API judge.

QUOTES
- p.1 abstract: "SkillComposer raises the pass rate by {+23.1, +18.2}pp over the no-skill baseline, surpassing top-3 retrieval and matching the gold-skill retrieval upper bound at lower prompt-token cost."
- p.9: "Loading the entire library (All Skills) recovers only a small fraction of that headroom while inflating the Codex prompt to 1.27M input tokens, confirming that flooding the context is not enough."

LIMITS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW
- The library is closed and fixed at 196 skills. It is not tested on open or online-updated libraries.
- Training data are mostly synthetic: 9,872 records, only 65 real anchors, with Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro generating the rest. The ordering ground truth is partly Gemini-generated.
- Downstream margins are small and not significance-tested. SkillComposer is 1.3 pp above top-3 retrieval on Codex (45.3 vs 44.0), with 225 trials and no confidence intervals. It is still below Gold Skills (51.1 / 48.4). On Gemini it is 2.2 pp above top-3 (44.0 vs 41.8).
- Skills are injected into the prompt up front, so this does not test mid-task, progressive-disclosure loading.
- The ablations do not isolate ordering's contribution to pass rate. There is no shuffled-order control for downstream results.
- The case studies show one case where Gold Skills scored 0.00 and SkillComposer 1.00. They show a short-sequence bias: it under-emits by one skill on long-chain tasks (lean4-proof). Retrieval scored 1.00 there, and SFT is slightly better at k≥3.
- On the real holdout, SkillComposer's Set F1 (62.9) is below oracle-k TF-IDF (74.2) and only ~2 pp above best-k TF-IDF.
- The real-anchor column in the per-layer table has n=4, standard error above 0.25 (Table 6).
- 13 tasks were excluded because retrievers route them trivially. The code-oriented, text-only scope is conceded by the authors. Trained-model per-layer results were not saved.
- Setup is not reproducible from the text alone: α/β values differ between sections (1.0/0.5 in §4.3, 0.5/0.25 in §5.1).

BUILDS ON
- Closed-vocabulary generative retrieval and tool selection: Rajput et al. 2023 (NeurIPS, generative retrieval for recommenders); Hao et al. 2023 (ToolkenGPT, NeurIPS).
- SkillsBench (Li et al. 2026, arXiv:2602.12670), supplying the library, tasks and benchmark.
- Open Agent Skills standard (agentskills.io) and Anthropic 2025 (agent skills engineering post); SoK: Agentic Skills (Jiang et al. 2026, arXiv:2602.20867).
- Retrieval baselines: SkillFlow (Li et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.06188); Graph of Skills (Liu et al. 2026a, arXiv:2604.05333).
- Tool planning: HuggingGPT (Shen 2023), Toolformer (Schick 2023), Voyager-style skill libraries (Wang 2023).
- Harbor evaluation framework (2026).

Relevance: it supports 04-retrieval.md (skill/tool retrieval). Flat top-k retrieval is a strong baseline, and loading all skills hurts. A sparse lexical prior beat dense for short, specific skill names.
